drug_class: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (PD-L1 blocking antibody) / Cancer immunotherapy
purpose: Avelumab is a cancer medicine used to treat a rare type of skin cancer called Merkel cell carcinoma and a type of bladder or urinary tract cancer called urothelial carcinoma. It is used when the cancer has spread to other parts of the body or cannot be removed with surgery. It helps your own immune system fight the cancer cells.
how_it_works: Your immune system has natural 'brakes' that normally stop it from attacking your own body. Cancer cells can hijack one of these brakes, called PD-L1, to hide from your immune system. Avelumab blocks that brake, so your immune system can recognize and attack the cancer cells again.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or weak, nausea, decreased appetite, diarrhea, constipation, swelling in the arms or legs, urinary tract infections, cough, shortness of breath, and skin rash. Infusion reactions (chills, fever, flushing, low blood pressure) can happen during or shortly after the IV infusion.
warnings: Avelumab can cause your immune system to become overactive and attack healthy organs — this is called an immune-related reaction. This can affect your lungs, liver, intestines, kidneys, hormone glands, heart, or skin and can be serious or life-threatening. Tell your doctor right away if you have new or worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, severe diarrhea, yellowing of skin or eyes, unusual weight gain or loss, or severe skin reactions. It can also harm an unborn baby, so reliable birth control is important during treatment and for at least one month after the last dose.
typical_dosing: Avelumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion into a vein, usually over about one hour. The typical dose is 800 mg every two weeks. You will likely receive antihistamine and acetaminophen (Tylenol) beforehand to help prevent infusion reactions. Your doctor will decide how long you continue treatment based on how your body responds.
